	  (c) 	Plant and equipment
  (i)  Recognition and measurement
	   	 		Items of plant and equipment are stated at cost less accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment 
losses, if any.
	   	 		Cost includes expenditures that are directly attributable to the acquisition of the asset and any other costs 
directly attributable to bringing the asset to working condition for its intended use, and the costs of dismantling 
and removing the items and restoring the site on which they are located.
	  	 		Purchased software that is integral to the functionality of the related equipment is capitalised as part of 
that equipment.
	   	 		When significant parts of an item of plant and equipment have different useful lives, they are accounted for as 
separate items (major components) of plant and equipment.
	   	 		The gain and loss on disposal of an item of plant and equipment is determined by comparing the proceeds from 
disposal with the carrying amount of plant and equipment and is recognised net within “other non-operating 
income” and “other operating expenses” respectively in profit or loss.
  (ii)  Subsequent costs
	   	 		The cost of replacing part of an item of plant and equipment is recognised in the carrying amount of the item if 
it is probable that the future economic benefits embodied within the part will flow to the Group or the Trust and 
its cost can be measured reliably. The carrying amount of the replaced part is derecognised and is charged to 
profit or loss. The costs of the day-to-day servicing of equipment are recognised in profit or loss as incurred.
  (iii)  Depreciation
	   	 		Depreciation is based on the cost of an asset less its residual value. Significant parts of individual assets 
are assessed, and if a part has a useful life that is different from the remainder of that asset, then that part is 
depreciated separately.
	   	 		Depreciation is recognised in profit or loss on a straight-line basis over the estimated useful lives of each part 
of an item of plant and equipment from the date that they are available for use.
	   	 	 The estimated useful lives for the current and comparative periods are as follows:
			Computer 					2 - 3 years
	   	 	 Office and other equipment 		   3 - 5 years
	   	 		Depreciation methods, useful lives and residual values are reassessed at the end of the reporting period, and 
adjusted as appropriate.
	  (d)	Investment properties
	   	 		Investment properties are properties which are owned or held under leasehold interest to earn rental income 
or for capital appreciation or for both, but not for sale in the ordinary course of business, used in the production 
or supply of goods or services or for administrative purposes. Investment properties are measured initially at 
cost and subsequently at fair value with any changes therein recognised in profit or loss for the period in which 
they arise. Cost includes expenditure that is directly attributable to the acquisition of the investment properties.
	   	 		Fair value is determined in accordance with the Deed and the REIT Guidelines which requires the investment 
properties to be valued by independent professional valuers. In determining the fair value, the valuers used 
valuation techniques which involve certain estimates. In relying on the valuation reports, the Manager has 
exercised its judgement and is satisfied that the valuation methods and estimates reflect the current market 
conditions. The fair value is determined annually based on independent professional valuation.

	  (e)	Leases
	   	 		At inception of a contract, the Group assesses whether a contract is, or contains, a lease. A contract is, or 
contains, a lease if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time 
in exchange for consideration.
  (i)  As a lessee
	   	 		At commencement or on modification of a contract that contains a lease component, the Group allocates the 
consideration in the contract to each lease component on the basis of its relative stand-alone prices. However, 
for the leases of property, the Group has elected not to separate non-lease components and account for the 
lease and non-lease components as a single lease component.
	   	 		The Group recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability at the lease commitment date. The right-of-use 
asset is initially measured at cost, which comprises the initial amount of the lease liability adjusted for any lease 
payments made at or before the commencement date, plus any initial direct costs incurred and an estimate of 
costs to dismantle and remove the underlying asset or to restore the underlying asset or the site on which it is 
located, less any lease incentives received.
	   	 		The right-of-use asset is subsequently depreciated using the straight-line method from the commencement 
date to the end of the lease term, unless the lease transfers ownership of the underlying asset to the Group by 
the end of the lease term or the cost of the right-of-use asset reflects that the Group will exercise a purchase 
option. In that case, the right-of-use asset will be depreciated over the useful life of the underlying asset, which 
is determined on the same basis as those of property and equipment. In addition, the right-of-use asset is 
periodically reduced by impairment losses, if any, and adjusted for certain remeasurements of the lease liability.
	   	 		The lease liability is initially measured at the present value of the lease payments that are not paid at the 
commencement date, discounted using the interest rate implicit in the lease or, if that rate cannot be readily 
determined, the lessee’s incremental borrowing rate.
   Short-term leases and leases of low-value assets
	   	 		The Group has elected not to recognise right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for leases of low-value assets 
and short-term leases, including office equipment. The Group recognises the lease payments associated with 
these leases as an expense on a straight-line basis over the lease term.
  (ii)  As a lessor
	  	 		At inception or on modification of a contract that contains a lease component, the Group allocates the 
consideration in the contract to each lease component on the basis of their relative stand-alone prices.
	   	 		When the Group acts as a lessor, it determines at lease inception whether each lease is a finance lease or an 
operating lease.
	   	 		To classify each lease, the Group makes an overall assessment of whether the lease transfers substantially 
all of the risks and rewards incidental to ownership of the underlying asset. If this is the case, then the lease 
is a finance lease; if not, then it is an operating lease. As part of this assessment, the Group considers certain 
indicators such as whether the lease is for the major part of the economic life of the asset.

	   	 		A financial asset or a financial liability is recognised in the statement of financial position when, and only when,

  (ii)  Financial instrument categories and subsequent measurement
   Financial assets
	   	 		Categories of financial assets are determined on initial recognition and are not reclassified subsequent to their 
initial recognition unless the Group or the Trust changes its business model for managing financial assets in 
which case all affected financial assets are reclassified on the first day of the first reporting period following 
the change of the business model.
   Amortised cost

Amortised cost category comprises financial assets that are held within a business model whose objective is 
to hold assets to collect contractual cash flows and its contractual terms give rise on specified dates to cash 
flows that are solely payments of principal and interest on the principal amount outstanding. The financial 
assets are not designated as fair value through profit or loss. Subsequent to initial recognition, these financial 
assets are measured at amortised cost using the effective interest method. The amortised cost is reduced by 
impairment losses. Interest income, foreign exchange gains and losses and impairment are recognised in profit 
or loss. Any gain or loss on derecognition is recognised in profit or loss.
	   	 		Interest income is recognised by applying effective interest rate to the gross carrying amount except for credit 
impaired financial assets (see Note 2(g)(i)) where the effective interest rate is applied to the amortised cost.
	   	 		Financial assets of the Group and of the Trust are subject to impairment assessment in accordance with Note 
2(g)(i).
   Financial liabilities and equity instruments
   Classification as debt or equity
	   	 		Financial liabilities and equity instruments issued by the Group and the Trust are classified according to the 
substance of the contractual arrangements entered into and the definitions of a financial liability and an 
equity instrument.
   Financial liabilities
	   	 		The financial liabilities at initial recognition of the Group and of the Trust are classified as amortised cost. 
Financial liabilities are subsequently measured at amortised cost using the effective interest method.
	   	 		Interest expense and foreign exchange gains and losses are recognised in profit or loss. Any gains or losses 
on derecognition are also recognised in profit or loss.

   Equity instruments
	   	 		An equity instrument is any contract that evidences a residual interest in the assets of an entity after deducting 
all of its liabilities. Equity instruments issued by the Group and the Trust are recognised at the proceeds received, 
net of direct issue costs.
	   	 		Instruments classified as equity are measured at cost on initial recognition and are not remeasured subsequently. 
Costs directly attributable to the issue of instruments classified as equity are recognised as a deduction 
from equity.
  (iii)  Derecognition
	   	 		A financial asset or part of it is derecognised when, and only when the contractual rights to the cash flows 
from the financial asset expire or transferred, or control of the asset is not retained or substantially all of the 
risks and rewards of ownership of the financial asset are transferred to another party. On derecognition of a 
financial asset, the difference between the carrying amount of the financial asset and the sum of consideration 
received (including any new asset obtained less any new liability assumed) is recognised in profit or loss.
	   	 		A financial liability or a part of it is derecognised when, and only when, the obligation specified in the contract 
is discharged, cancelled or expires. A financial liability is also derecognised when its terms are modified and 
the cash flows of the modified liability are substantially different, in which case, a new financial liability based 
on modified terms is recognised at fair value. On derecognition of a financial liability, the difference between 
the carrying amount of the financial liability extinguished or transferred to another party and the consideration 
paid, including any non-cash assets transferred or liabilities assumed, is recognised in profit or loss.
  (iv)  Offsetting
	   	 		Financial assets and financial liabilities are offset and the net amount presented in the statement of financial 
position when, and only when, the Group and the Trust currently have a legally enforceable right to set off the 
amounts and they intend either to settle them on a net basis or to realise the asset and liability simultaneously.
	  (g)	Impairment
  (i)  Financial assets
	   	 		The Group and the Trust recognise loss allowances for expected credit losses on financial assets measured 
at amortised cost. Expected credit losses are a probability-weighted estimate of credit losses.
	   	 		The Group and the Trust measure loss allowances for trade receivables at an amount equal to lifetime expected 
credit loss. For all other financial instruments, the Group and the Trust recognise lifetime expected credit loss 
when there has been a significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition. However, if the credit risk on the 
financial instrument has not increased significantly since initial recognition, the Group and the Trust measure 
the loss allowance for that financial instrument at an amount equal to 12-month expected credit loss.
	   	 		When determining whether the credit risk of a financial asset has increased significantly since the initial 
recognition and when estimating expected credit loss, the Group and the Trust consider reasonable and 
supportable information that is relevant and available without undue cost or effort. This includes both 
quantitative and qualitative information and analysis, based on the Group’s historical experience and informed 
credit assessment and including forward-looking information, where available.

	   	 		Lifetime expected credit losses are the expected credit losses that result from all possible default events over 
the expected life of the asset, while 12-month expected credit losses are the portion of expected credit losses 
that result from default events that are possible within the 12 months after the reporting date. The maximum 
period considered when estimating expected credit losses is the maximum contractual period over which the 
Group and the Trust are exposed to credit risk.
	   	 		The Group and the Trust estimate the expected credit losses on trade receivables by assessing the risk of loss

ratings, where applicable.
	   	 		An impairment loss in respect of financial assets measured at amortised cost is recognised in profit or loss and 
the carrying amount of the asset is reduced through the use of an allowance account.
	   	 		At each reporting date, the Group and the Trust assess whether financial assets carried at amortised cost are 
credit impaired. A financial asset is credit impaired when one or more events that have a detrimental impact 
on the estimated future cash flows of the financial asset have occurred.
	   	 		The gross carrying amount of a financial asset is written off (either partially or full) to the extent that there is no 
realistic prospect of recovery. This is generally the case when the Group or the Trust determines that the debtor 
does not have assets or sources of income that could generate sufficient cash flows to repay the amounts 
subject to the write-off. However, financial assets that are written off could still be subject to enforcement 
activities in order to comply with the Group’s or the Trust’s procedures for recovery of amounts due.
  (ii)  Other assets
	   	 		The carrying amounts of other assets, other than investment properties, are reviewed at the end of each 
reporting date to determine whether there is any indication of impairment. If any such indication exists, then 
the asset’s recoverable amount is estimated.
	   	 		For the purpose of impairment testing, assets are grouped together into the smallest group of assets that 
generates cash inflows from continuing use that are largely independent of the cash inflows of other assets.
	   	 		The recoverable amount of an asset is the greater of its value in use and its fair value less costs of disposal. In 
assessing value in use, the estimated future cash flows are discounted to their present value using a pre-tax 
discount rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to 
the asset.
	   	 		An impairment loss is recognised if the carrying amount of an asset exceeds its estimated recoverable amount. 
Impairment loss is recognised in profit or loss.
	   	 		Impairment losses recognised in prior periods are assessed at the end of each reporting period for any 
indications that the loss has decreased or no longer exists. An impairment loss is reversed if there has been 
a change in the estimates used to determine the recoverable amount since the last impairment loss was 
recognised. An impairment loss is reversed only to the extent that the asset’s carrying amount does not exceed 
the carrying amount that would have been determined, net of depreciation or amortisation, if no impairment 
loss had been recognised. Reversals of impairment losses are credited to profit or loss in the financial year in 
which the reversals are recognised.

	  (m)	Tax expense
	   	 	 Tax expense comprises current and deferred tax. Current tax and deferred tax are recognised in profit or loss.
	   	 		Current tax is the expected tax payable or receivable on the taxable income or loss for the year, using tax rates 
enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period, and any adjustment to tax payable or 
receivable in respect of previous financial years.
	   	 		Deferred tax is recognised using the liability method, providing for temporary differences between the carrying 
amounts of assets and liabilities in the statements of financial position and their tax bases. Deferred tax is not 
recognised for the initial recognition of assets or liabilities in a transaction that is not a business combination 
and that affects neither accounting nor taxable profit or loss. Deferred tax is measured at the tax rates that 
are expected to be applied to the temporary differences when they reverse, based on the laws that have been 
enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period.
	   	 		Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset if there is a legally enforceable right to offset current tax liabilities 
and assets, and they relate to taxes levied by the same tax authority on the same taxable entity.	
	   	 		A deferred tax asset is recognised to the extent that it is probable that future taxable profits will be available 
against which the temporary difference can be utilised. Deferred tax assets are reviewed at each reporting 
period and are reduced to the extent that it is no longer probable that the related tax benefit will be realised.
	   	 		Where investment properties are carried at fair value in accordance with the accounting policy set out in Note 
2(d), the amount of deferred tax recognised is measured using the tax rates that would apply on the sale of 
those assets at their carrying values at the reporting date unless the property is depreciable and is held with 
the objective to consume substantially all the economic benefits embodied in the property over time, rather 
than through sale. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are not discounted.
	  (n)	Earnings per unit
	   	 		The Group and the Trust present basic and diluted earnings per unit. Basic earnings per unit is calculated by 
dividing the total return by the weighted average number of units outstanding during the financial year. Diluted 
earnings per unit is determined by adjusting the total return and the weighted average number of ordinary units 
outstanding, for the effects of all dilutive potential units.
	  (o)	Operating segments
	   	 		An operating segment is a component of the Group that engages in business activities from which it may 
earn revenues and incur expenses, including revenues and expenses that relate to transactions with any of 
the Group’s other components. All operating segments’ results are reviewed and used by the Group’s Chief 
Operating Decision Makers for strategic decision making and resources allocation.

(p)	Fair value measurements
	   	 		Fair value of an asset or a liability, except for lease transactions, is determined as the price that would be 
received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the 
measurement date. The measurement assumes that the transaction to sell the asset or transfer the liability takes 
place either in the principal market or in the absence of a principal market, in the most advantageous market.
	   	 		For non-financial asset, the fair value measurement takes into account a market participant’s ability to generate 
economic benefits by using the asset in its highest and best use or by selling it to another market participant 
that would use the asset in its highest and best use.
	   	 		When measuring the fair value of an asset or a liability, the Group uses observable market data as far as possible. 
Fair value are categorised into different levels in a fair value hierarchy based on the input used in the valuation 
technique as follows:
	   	 		Level 1:		quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities that the Group can access 
at the measurement date.
	   	 	 Level 2:		inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1 that are observable for the asset or liability, 
either directly or indirectly.
	   	 	 Level 3:		unobservable inputs for the asset or liability.
	   	 		The Group recognises transfers between the levels of the fair value hierarchy as of the date of the event or 
change in circumstances that caused the transfers.

(b)	Fair value information
	   	The fair value of investment properties of the Group and of the Trust are categorised as Level 3. The properties 
are valued by independent external valuers using the income capitalisation approach, also known as investment 
approach. This valuation approach takes into account the gross revenue and outgoings to estimate the net income 
for the properties. Capitalisation rates are then applied to the net income of the investment properties to determine 
the market value of the investment properties.
	   	The significant assumptions and unobservable inputs underlying the estimation of fair value of investment properties 
are those related to term capitalisation and reversionary capitalisation rates, car park and other income, outgoings 
expenses and allowance for void. Term capitalisation and reversionary capitalisation rates for the investment 
properties range from 6.00% to 7.25% (FY 2024: 6.00% to 7.25%) and from 6.25% to 7.50% (FY 2024: 6.25% to 
7.50%) respectively. The estimated fair value would increase (decrease) if the capitalisation rates, outgoings and 
allowance for void were lower (higher) and if car park and other income was higher (lower).

23.3	 Financial risk management
	   		Financial risk management is integral to the whole business of the Group and of the Trust. The Group and the 
Trust adopt an integrated approach to manage the financial risks arising in the normal course of business.
	   	 The Group and the Trust have identified the following financial risk exposure from its use of financial instruments:
•  	 Liquidity risk
•  	 Credit risk
•  	 Market risk
	   		The Group and the Trust have implemented risk management policies and guidelines which set its tolerance of 
risk and its general risk management philosophy.
23.4	Liquidity risk
	   		Liquidity risk is defined as the risk that the Group and the Trust will not be able to meet its financial obligations as 
they fall due.
	   		The Group’s and the Trust’s exposures to liquidity risk arise primarily from various payables and borrowings. The

Group and the Trust maintain sufficient liquid reserves in terms of cash and credit facilities to ensure, as far as 
possible, that they will have sufficient liquidity to meet its liabilities when they fall due. In addition, the Manager 
diligently monitors and observes financing covenants to ensure compliance.
	   		The health and sentiments of the debt markets in Malaysia directly affects the liquidity position of the Group and 
the Trust as external sources of funding are needed to fund new acquisitions or asset enhancement initiatives 
besides the need to refinance the existing borrowings when they mature.
	   		At the reporting date, RM119,125,000 (FY 2024: RM185,126,000) of outstanding revolving credits will be subject 
to annual review within the next twelve months. The Group and the Trust will continue to manage their capital 
structure proactively by spreading out the debt maturities to a manageable size and maintaining an optimal 
gearing level.
	   		It is not expected that the cash flows included in the maturity analysis could occur significantly earlier or at 
significantly different amounts.

23.5	 Credit risk
	   		Credit risk is defined as the risk of a financial loss to the Group and to the Trust if a customer or counterparty to 
a financial instrument fails to meet its contractual obligations. The Group’s and the Trust’s exposures to credit 
risk arise primarily from their trade and other receivables.
	   		Credit risk is controlled by credit verification procedures before lease agreements are entered into with tenants 
and ongoing balance monitoring to ensure minimum credit risk exposure. In addition, there is a stringent collection 
policy in place to ensure that credit risk is minimised. Other than the collection of security deposits, which typically 
amounts to an average of three months’ rent in the form of cash or bankers’ guarantee, the Group and the Trust 
also have vigilant monitoring and debt collection procedures. Additionally, certain revenue streams such as car 
park income and recovery from tenants do not have credit terms since they are settled on cash or prepayment 
terms. Debtors turnover days of the Group for the financial year was approximately 9 days (FY 2024: 11 days).
	   		For other financial assets, the Group and the Trust minimise credit risk by dealing with restricted counterparties 
that meet the appropriate credit criteria and have high credit standing.
	   		The Manager establishes an allowance for impairment that represents its estimate of incurred losses in respect 
of trade and other receivables. The main component of this allowance is a specific loss component that relates 
to the individually significant exposure. The allowance account in respect of trade and other receivables is used 
to record impairment losses unless the Manager is satisfied that no recovery of the amount owing is possible. 
At that point, the financial asset is considered irrecoverable and the amount charged to the allowance account 
is written off against the carrying amount of the impaired financial asset.
	   		At the end of financial year, there was no significant concentration of credit risk.
	   	 Cash and bank balances are placed with financial institutions which are regulated.
23.6	Market risk
	   		Market risk is the risk that changes in market prices, such as foreign exchange rates, interest rates and other 
prices that will affect the Group’s and the Trust’s financial positions or cash flows.
     23.6.1Interest rate risk
	   		The Group’s and the Trust’s investments in financial products and its fixed rate borrowings are exposed to a 
risk of change in the fair values of the instruments due to changes in interest rates. The Group’s and the Trust’s 
floating rate borrowings are exposed to a risk of change in cash flows due to changes in interest rate. Short term 
receivables and payables are not significantly exposed to interest rate risk. Of these instruments, the primary 
interest rate risk exposure of the Group and of the Trust relates to interest-bearing borrowings.
	   		In line with the Group’s overall enterprise risk management framework, the Manager adopts a proactive interest 
rate management policy to manage the risk associated with changes in interest rates on the Group’s and the 
Trust’s loan facilities (including borrowing from subsidiary) and also seeking to ensure a competitive level of 
cost of debt. Interest rate risk is managed on an ongoing basis with the primary objective of limiting the extent to 
which interest expense could be affected by adverse movements in interest rates.
	   		To mitigate the Group’s exposure to fluctuation in interest rates, the Manager has locked in a proportion of the 
Group’s and the Trust’s borrowings at fixed interest rates. As at 31 December 2025, the Group’s and the Trust’s 
borrowings at fixed rates are 84.0% (FY 2024: 85.0%) while the remaining balances are on floating rates.
	   		The investments in financial products are mainly short-term in nature and not held for trading or speculative 
purposes but are mainly placed as deposits with licensed banks which yield better returns than cash at bank.

The Group and the Trust own a portfolio of investment properties comprising shopping malls, logistics and industrial 
assets located in Malaysia. Investment properties represent the single largest category of assets on the statements

of financial position, at RM5,490,300,000 and RM5,484,300,000 of the Group and of the Trust respectively as at 31 
December 2025.
These investment properties are stated at their fair values based on independent external valuations.
The valuation process involves significant judgement in determining the appropriate valuation methodology to be used, 
and in estimating the underlying assumptions to be applied. The valuations are highly sensitive to key assumptions applied 
such as the capitalisation rates i.e. a small change in the assumptions can have a significant impact to the valuation.
This is a key audit matter because of the inherently subjective nature of investment property valuations arising from 
the use of assumptions in the valuation methodology and the financial significance of those balances to the Group and 
the Trust.

How the matter was addressed in our audit

•    	We evaluated the qualifications, competency, independence and objectivity of the external valuers.

the investment properties and assessed whether such methodology is consistent with those used in the industry.
•    	We interviewed the external valuers to understand their processes, judgements and observations in determining 
the property related data used as input and assumptions applied in their valuations.

1.1		   	Macroeconomic & Demographic 
Overview
The Malaysian economy expanded by 6.3% in 4Q 2025 
(4Q 2024: 4.9%), supported by sustained household 
spending amid positive labour market conditions, strong 
investment growth, growing exports growth led by exports 
of electrical & electronics (E&E) goods and information and 
communication technology (ICT)-related services, as well 
as robust tourism activity. Overall, the economy grew 5.2% 
in 2025 (2024: 5.1%).
Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) projects economic growth in 
2026 to be between 4.0% to 4.5%, supported by resilient 
domestic demand and exports. Household spending is 
expected to remain supported by positive labour market 
condition, alongside policy measures. Investment activity 
is anticipated to be driven by the progress of multi-year 
projects across both the private and public sectors, the 
continued realisation of approved investments, and the 
implementation of national master plans. Export growth 
will be underpinned by steady global demand, particularly 
for E&E goods. Additionally, increased tourism activities 
following the launch of Visit Malaysia Year 2026 will also 
support growth.
Labour market conditions remained stable, as the 
unemployment rate improved to 2.9% in December 2025, 
improving from 3.2% in 2024. Employment rose by 4.6% 
YoY to 17.1 million, reflecting sustained labour demand 
across major sectors, including services, manufacturing 
and construction. Labour supply also remained healthy, 
with the labour force participation rate edging up to 70.9% 
in (2024: 70.6%). In terms of demographics, preliminary 
figures estimate Malaysia’s population have increased 
0.5% YoY to 34.2 million in 2025.
Inflation remained stable, recording 1.4% in 2025 (2024: 
1.8%). Domestic policy reforms implemented during the 
year, including the expansion of the Sales and Service Tax

(SST)
1
 and adjustments to utility tariffs, were reported to 
have had a modest overall impact on price levels. Looking 
ahead, the Ministry of Finance Economic Report 2026 
projects headline inflation to range between 1.3% and 
2.0% in 2026.
Household income in Malaysia remained resilient in 2024, 
supporting consumer spending and broader economic 
activity.  According  to  the  Household  Income  and 
Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2024, mean monthly household 
income reached RM9,155 in Malaysia, reflecting a 3.9% 
CAGR since 2022, underpinned by income growth across 
the economy. Urban households saw stronger gains, 
with earnings averaging RM10,145 across the country. 
Disposable household income averaged RM7,584, up 
3.2% from 2022, indicating that a substantial portion 
of earnings remains available for both essential and 
discretionary expenditure.
In terms of monetary policy, BNM Monetary Policy 
Committee (MPC) maintained the Overnight Policy Rate 
(OPR) at 2.75% during its January 2026 meeting, following 
a reduction from 3.00% in July 2025. This marked the 
third consecutive meeting where the policy rate was left 
unchanged, with BNM assessing the stance as supportive 
of economic growth while remaining consistent with 
prevailing inflation and growth conditions.
Meanwhile, tourism activity continued to strengthen, with 
Malaysia recording 26.6 million tourist arrivals in 2025, 
representing an increase in 6.4% from 2024. Visitor 
arrivals were largely driven by neighbouring ASEAN 
markets, led by Singapore, China, Indonesia, Thailand 
and India. Looking ahead, preparations for Visit Malaysia 
2026 are underway, with the campaign targeting 47 million 
international visitors.

2.6		 Retail Market Outlook 
The retail market is expected to remain resilient, underpinned by steady employment conditions, moderated inflation 
and easing financing costs following recent monetary policy adjustments. A firmer Ringgit Malaysia (RM), together with 
sustained job creation across major urban centres, has supported household spending capacity. Demand continues to 
be anchored by essential retail and everyday F&B trade categories across mall formats.
According to Retail Group Malaysia (RGM), retail sales outperformed expectations in 3Q 2025, growing by 4.9% YoY, 
underpinned by resilient private consumption despite rising retail prices for groceries and discretionary goods. As a 
result, RGM upgraded its full-year retail sales forecast to 3.6% in 2025, supported by continued government cash 
assistance, civil servant salary adjustments and lower fuel prices. Looking ahead, RGM projects retail sales to grow by 
4.0% in 2026, supported by ongoing fiscal support measures and the anticipated uplift from the Visit Malaysia Year 
(VMY) 2026 campaign.
In response to evolving retail demand, mall operators are increasingly sharpening asset-level strategies to reinforce 
relevance within their respective catchments, with a clearer emphasis on experience-led attractions, stronger 
essentials anchoring and community-oriented tenant curation. Experience-driven concepts, including large-format 
indoor attractions and live event venues, are being introduced to support dwell time and broaden catchment appeal, 
as seen with the GameON Theme Park and Kin+Zo Land in The Mines and Idea Live Arena in 3 Damansara. In parallel, 
enhancements to supermarket and value-led anchors continue to underpin daily visitation, including a refreshed Cold

Storage at Sungei Wang Plaza, while selective tenant remixing and targeted marketing efforts, such as at East Coast 
Mall in Pahang and Gurney Plaza in Penang – reflect a more catchment-led approach to retail asset management.
At the consumer level, AI is reshaping retail discovery and purchasing patterns, with 58% of Malaysian consumers 
using AI tools, according to the Adyen Retail Report 2025; alongside evidence from Lazada, which has reported higher 
engagement and order values following the introduction of its AI-enabled shopping assistant. In parallel, retailers such 
as the newly launched Xiaomi Store at The Exchange TRX and Nanjing Dajing Que Tang Yu Fang in Pavilion Bukit Jalil are 
adopting smarter omnichannel models that integrate physical and digital channels through IoT-enabled and AI-driven 
experiential formats, signalling a shift towards more data-led, experience-oriented retail environments.
In the Klang Valley, recent retail completions such as KLGCC Mall and Sunway Square Mall illustrate this trend, reflecting 
a move towards integrated, community-focused formats that prioritise lifestyle offerings, convenience, and placemaking 
over traditional big-box concepts. These malls feature experiential attractions, F&B-led anchors, supermarkets, and 
mixed-use integration to support diversified and resilient footfall. At the same time, the concentration of new supply 
within a relatively short period may lead to overlapping catchments, prompting more selective tenant demand and 
heightened competition among malls.
In Penang, the upcoming Waterfront Shoppes  in 2026 is expected to intensify competition among prime retail assets on 
the island. Nevertheless, the market is projected to remain broadly stable, supported by sustained consumer spending, 
the continued entry of new retail brands, and positive spillover effects from state-level tourism initiatives as well as 
national campaigns such as VMY 2026.

3.1		 Market Overview
In 2025, Malaysia’s industrial landscape was shaped by an increasingly complex global trade environment, where 
heightened tariff pressures and geopolitical uncertainties prompted businesses to reassess supply chains and export 
strategies. Manufacturers and exporters faced cost and competitiveness challenges as elevated trade policy risks 
added to existing operational pressures, encouraging firms to diversify export markets and strengthen regional supply 
chain links.
Nevertheless, the Industrial Production Index (IPI) rose 3.6% YoY to 136.9 in 2025, marginally slower than the growth 
rate recorded over the same period in 2024. Growth continued to be driven by the manufacturing sector, which rose 
4.5% YoY, supported by sustained expansion in export-oriented industries, particularly the manufacture of computer, 
electronics and optical products.
Manufacturing output continued to be underpinned by export-oriented industries, supported by firm external demand, 
particularly for electronics and selected resource-based products. Recent months indicated improving momentum 
in export-linked manufacturing activity, broadly aligned with stronger manufactured exports. Domestic-oriented 
industries also recorded steady expansion, driven mainly by food processing and metal-related activities.

Approved Manufacturing Investment
As of 9M 2025, Malaysia recorded RM285.2 billion in total approved investments, marking a 13.2% YoY growth. Spanning 
4,874 projects across key sectors, these investments demonstrate Malaysia’s continued investment resilience amid 
global economic headwinds and reflects strong investor confidence in the nation’s long-term economic direction. Of 
the total approved investments, domestic investments accounted for RM134.4 billion, representing 47.1%, while foreign 
investments contributed RM150.8 billion, or 52.9%.
Malaysia’s manufacturing sector also demonstrated continued strength, securing RM93.8 billion in approved investments 
across 885 projects, which made up 32.9% of total approved investments in 9M 2025. Within this, foreign investments 
led with RM73.1 billion, representing 77.9% of total manufacturing investments, while domestic investments remained 
significant at RM20.7 billion, or 22.1%. Top performing industries included electrical and electronics (E&E), chemical 
and chemical products and transport equipment.
By state, Johor led approved manufacturing investments, accounting for 19.9% of the national total and rising 132.8% 
YoY to RM18.6 billion, supported by the Johor–Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) and the state’s strategic 
proximity to one of Asia’s most advanced economies. Penang followed with RM15.8 billion in approved manufacturing

investments, representing 16.8% of the total and increasing 30.0% YoY, underpinned by its mature electronics ecosystem. 
In contrast, Klang Valley (WP Kuala Lumpur and Selangor) saw a decline in approved manufacturing investments, down 
30.0% YoY to RM10.7 billion, contributing 11.5% of the national total.

3.3		 Industrial Property Sector: WP Kuala Lumpur & Selangor
Policy & Infrastructure 
Selangor has launched the IoT-Enabled Industrial Park (IEIP) initiative to accelerate Industry 4.0 adoption across selected 
industrial parks, promoting the integration of IoT, AI, automation and smart utilities. The IEIP is intended to support 
high-value industries, enhance operational efficiency and sustainability, and strengthen Selangor’s attractiveness to 
domestic and foreign investors.

The East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) is also progressing on schedule and is expected to be 90% complete by December 
2026, with operations expected to begin in 2027 from Kota Bahru to Gombak, Selangor. Upon completion, the ECRL is 
expected to strengthen the state’s competitiveness as a regional distribution hub, lowering logistics costs and improving 
supply chain efficiency.
At present, the West Coast Expressway (WCE) is partially operational, with several remaining sections in Selangor, 
including the Shah Alam Expressway (SAE) (Section 3) and Assam Jawa (Section 7), still under construction. Full 
completion is targeted by 1Q2027.

Notable Developments in the Industrial & Logistic Sectors
Klang Valley continues to strengthen its position as a key logistics and industrial hub in Malaysia, driven by a mix of global 
occupier investments, domestic strategic projects and industrial park expansions. Major supply chain investments such 
as YCH Group’s investment in Sime Darby’s Supply Chain City Malaysia in Bandar Bukit Raja and Nestlé’s integrated 
logistics hub at Port Klang reflect growing demand for high-specification, technology-enabled distribution infrastructure.
Meanwhile, collaboration between industrial players is extending into smart logistics infrastructure beyond traditional 
warehousing models. Chin Hin’s joint venture with PTT Synergy, and SP Setia’s collaboration with Taiwan’s Ally Logistic 
Property Co Ltd (ALP) to develop smart warehouses and digital logistics platforms signals broader adoption of automation 
and data-driven operations, a trend that is expected to enhance service quality and attract technology-driven tenants.
Global logistics operators are also deepening their footprint in the Klang Valley. This is seen with Maersk’s recent opening 
of its Mega Distribution Centre in Shah Alam which adds significant pallet capacity and automation capability, while Jaya 
Grocer’s investment of over RM100 million in a new automated warehouse highlights the increasing domestic uptake 
of advanced logistics solutions tailored for retail and FMCG supply chains.
In addition, strategic industrial park announcements such as the set up of the Chery Smart Auto Industrial Park in Hulu 
Selangor and the launch of Selangor Aero Park @ KLIA Aeropolis are further enhancing the investment narrative for Klang 
Valley. The Malaysia Semiconductor Integrated Circuit (IC) Design Park 2 in Cyberjaya was also launched, strengthening 
the region’s position as a potential regional semiconductor hub.
3.4		 Industrial Property Sector: Penang
Policy & Infrastructure
Penang continues to progress key infrastructure initiatives that are expected to support industrial and economic activity. 
The expansion of Penang International Airport (PIA) is advancing steadily, and the overall project remains on track for 
completion by 2028. The upgrade includes apron expansions, taxiway rehabilitation and ancillary buildings – capabilities 
that will benefit export-oriented manufacturing and logistics operations in the northern region.

Independent Market Overview
In parallel, the construction of the Penang Mutiara Light Rail Transit (LRT) project is scheduled to begin early 2026. 
Spanning 29.5km with 21 strategically located stations, the line connects key locations including the Penang Silicon 
Island, Penang International Airport, Bayan Lepas Free Industrial Zone, and George Town – improving accessibility 
between industrial nodes, logistics hubs and urban centres.
Meanwhile, reclamation and infrastructure development at the Penang Silicon Island continues to make progress, with 
more than 80 hectares reclaimed to date and phased connectivity improvements planned via the forthcoming Pan Island 
Link 2A (PIL2A) highway and bridge link, enhancing land supply for future industrial and mixed-use development.
Industrial Supply
As of 9M 2025, Penang’s cumulative industrial supply stood at 9,974 units – with the majority comprising terraced 
(53.0%), semi-detached (20.7%) and detached factories (20.1%). Incoming supply totalled 223 units, with the majority 
comprising semi-detached factories (67.7% or 151 units), followed by detached factories (23.3% or 52 units) and 
terraced factories (8.1% or 18 units).

Notable Developments in the Industrial & Logistic Sectors
Penang’s industrial landscape is advancing on multiple fronts, anchored by strategic public–private collaborations and 
major infrastructure initiatives. In Seberang Perai, S P Setia and the Penang Development Corporation (PDC) will jointly 
develop approximately 350 acres within the Setia Fontaines township into a green-themed industrial park.
Additionally, the Silicon Island project has unveiled Phase 1 of the Green Tech Park – the flagship industrial precinct of 
the project. The project is on track to welcome the construction of the first factories in 2026, with operations to begin 
as early as 2027.
Penang’s logistics ecosystem is also gaining momentum with developments at the Penang International Logistics 
Aeropark (PILA), a 42-hectare future-ready air cargo and logistics hub planned adjacent to Penang International Airport. 
PDC has signed memorandums of understanding (MoUs) with global logistics operators FedEx and DHL to establish 
integrated logistics and air freight facilities within PILA.
Global logistics service providers are also strengthening their footprint in Penang. UPS has opened a new 20,000 sq ft 
package centre in Penang Science Park North and expanded its airport hub to boost processing capacity and delivery 
efficiency for express and freight services. Furthermore, Sin-Kung Logistics Berhad has signed an MoU with PDC to 
explore the possibility of leasing within PILA in bids to strengthen its operations in Penang.
3.5		 Industrial Property Sector: Johor
Policy & Infrastructure
The Johor–Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) remains a key catalyst for Johor’s industrial market, supported 
by targeted incentives aimed at attracting high-value manufacturing and services activities. Key measures include 
preferential tax rates for qualifying investments and knowledge workers, fast-tracked regulatory approvals via the Invest 
Malaysia Facilitation Centre–Johor, and enhanced funding support for talent development and strategic co-investment. 
Together with improving cross-border connectivity and logistics infrastructure, these initiatives are expected to 
strengthen Johor’s competitiveness as a regional industrial and investment hub.
Additionally, the Port of Tanjung Pelepas (PTP) is advancing its expansion plans with the development of a new berth 
to increase handling capacity over the next few years. The port’s growth outlook is further strengthened by Maersk’s 
decision to designate PTP as its main transshipment hub in Asia. Reflecting this momentum, Alphaliner ranked PTP as 
the world’s fastest-growing port, recording a 15.4% growth rate in the first half of 2025.

Notable Developments in the Industrial & Logistic Sectors
Johor’s industrial property landscape continues to attract significant strategic investments and partnerships. A landmark 
development is the Eco Business Park 8 in Kulai, a 381.24-hectare integrated industrial park located within the Johor–
Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ). Other notable industrial parks include the MS Industrial Park @ Kulai – a 
419-acre joint venture project between Mah Sing Group Berhad and KLK Land, and MB World Group Bhd's 732-acre 
MBW Innexus Industrial City in Tanjung Langsat. The project is a freehold heavy industrial development with an estimated 
GDV of RM2.03 billion located within the Forest City Special Financial Zone (SFZ) under the JS-SEZ.
On the logistics front, Johor continues to attract strong interest from global supply chain operators. At 103° Free 
Commercial Zone in Sunway City Iskandar Puteri, Singapore-headquartered Equalbase and Sunway Group have 
secured full long-term lease commitments for Phase I. Global logistics provider DB Schenker Logistics has committed to 
approximately 830,000 sq ft of warehouse space, while GXO Logistics has taken the entire 720,000 sq ft of Warehouse 2. 
In addition, Barry Callebaut, in partnership with AP Moller–Maersk, has opened a purpose-built cocoa bean warehouse 
in Pasir Gudang, Johor, marking one of the largest cocoa storage facilities in the Asia Pacific region. 
Local logistics developers are also active: ISP Group has broken ground on its RM80 million ISP Victory logistics hub in 
Senai. Located on a 10.22-acre industrial site, the project comprises a dual-storey logistics and manufacturing facility 
with a total built-up area of approximately 263,000 sq ft..
Beyond parks and logistics hubs, notable manufacturing investments continue to reinforce Johor’s industrial base. 
Significant capital commitments include:
•    Gold Peak Technology Group’s RM670 million investment in advanced manufacturing and R&D in JS-SEZ;
•    Biocon Ltd’s RM1.1 billion investment in biopharmaceutical operations in Iskandar Malaysia;
•    FerroTec Power Semiconductor’s RM550 million investment in Pasir Gudang; and

• 
Southern Catalyst Sdn Bhd’s AgroPolis project aimed at enhancing agro-industrial capacity in Sedenak. The project 
is expected to draw up to RM500 million in investments.
These large-scale investments are expected to drive long-term demand for industrial space across various manufacturing 
and logistics segments.

3.6		 Industrial Market Outlook
Looking ahead, Malaysia’s industrial sector is expected 
to maintain its momentum, supported by improving 
global demand, particularly in the electronics and AI-
related segments and further supported by domestic 
policy measures. National frameworks such as the New 
Industrial Master Plan (NIMP) 2030, the National Energy 
Transition Roadmap (NETR) and the Johor–Singapore 
Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) are expected to enhance 
Malaysia’s competitiveness as a regional industrial and 
logistics hub.
Key infrastructure projects, including the East Coast Rail 
Link (ECRL), the West Coast Expressway (WCE) and 
Johor Bahru–Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) are 
anticipated to further enhance connectivity and support 
demand along strategic transport corridors. Strategic 
engagements and trade agreements are also expected to 
benefit major industrial hubs, boosting investor confidence 
and driving demand for logistics and high-specification 
industrial spaces. Recent trade developments include 
the signing of the Malaysia–EFTA Economic Partnership 
Agreement (MEEPA) with Switzerland, Norway, Iceland 
and Liechtenstein, followed by new agreements with New 
Zealand and South Korea, alongside the resumption of free 
trade negotiations with the European Union.
Increasingly, technology and sustainability adoption 
are becoming critical to the sector’s evolution. The 
deployment of 5G connectivity in industrial zones, growing 
adoption of AI and automation, and emphasis on green 
building practices are reshaping how industrial spaces 
are designed, operated, and valued. ESG-driven industrial 
developments, smart warehouses, and AI-enabled 
logistics hubs are emerging as top investment priorities, 
attracting both domestic and global tenants seeking 
sustainable and future-ready facilities.
The Klang Valley industrial market is expected to remain 
resilient, underpinned by its mature infrastructure, 
strategic location and deep concentration of modern, 
automation-ready industrial parks. Many of these 
developments are designed to support higher operational 
efficiency and sustainability, aligning with occupier 
demand from higher-value industrial segments such as 
advanced manufacturing, e-commerce logistics and 
semiconductor-related activities, which are expected to 
continue driving space absorption.
Meanwhile, Penang’s industrial sector continues to benefit 
from its strategic role in the E&E supply chain, ongoing 
infrastructure upgrades, and sustained investor interest. 
Major initiatives, including the Penang South reclamation 
project and the expansion of Penang International Airport, 
are expected to reinforce the State’s position as a key 
industrial hub, attracting high-value manufacturing and 
logistics investments. The strategic location of Penang 
within regional supply chains continues to underpin 
demand for modern industrial space, particularly with 
the development of new industrial parks such as Setia 
Fontaines and the Green Tech Park within Silicon Island.
Johor’s industrial sector is poised for sustained growth

with the Johor–Singapore Special Economic Zone 
(JS -SEZ) as a key structural driver of future investment 
and industrial land demand. The JS-SEZ’s targeted 
incentives, coupled with proactive co-investment and 
talent development support, are expected to attract 
high -value manufacturing, advanced logistics, and 
technology-intensive services, anchoring longer-term 
industrial growth in the southern corridor.
Beyond policy support, Johor’s evolving industrial 
landscape is characterised by a growing pipeline of 
strategic developments that reinforce its appeal to both 
global and domestic occupiers. Notable projects such as 
the Eco Business Park 8 and MS Industrial Park @ Kulai are 
enhancing modern industrial capacity, while major logistics 
leases point to strong demand for high-specification 
distribution and supply chain infrastructure. At the same 
time, significant manufacturing investments across various 
advanced manufacturing segments are broadening the 
state’s industrial base.

GHG Emissions Data Methodology
CLMT’s methodology for computing Scope 1, 2, and 3 GHG emissions are listed below.
GHG Emissions Data Methodology
ApproachCLMT computes Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions using Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate 
Accounting and Reporting Standard (2004), and Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Value 
Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard (2011), unless otherwise stated.
CLMT uses the operational control approach as defined by the GHG Protocol, and determined 
that it has operational control over the properties that CLI-operationally manages. 
Gases included in computation are carbon dioxide (CO
2
), methane (CH
4
), nitrous oxide 
(N₂O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), and sulphur hexafluoride 
(SF

6
), where applicable, and where the relevant emission factor inclusive of these gases is 
available in the emission factor databases used by CLMT.
Scope 1 GHG 	
emissions
Scope 1 GHG emissions relate to direct emissions from direct fuel combustion (Diesel). 
Emission and Conversion factors
UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 2025. 
Changes in reporting period
No changes.
Scope 2 GHG 	
emissions
Scope 2 GHG emissions relate to indirect emissions from purchased electricity. 
Emission and Conversion factors
IEA 2025 v1.1 (AR6 Applied). 
Changes in reporting period
No changes.
Scope 3 GHG 	
Emissions
Cat 3 Fuel- and energy-related activities
Relates to emissions from the production and transmission and distribution of fuels and 
energy consumed by CLMT, that are not accounted for in Scope 1 and 2. 
Emission and Conversion factors
WTT and transmission and distribution loss emission factors used for computation of 
emissions were from UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 
2025. UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 2021 where 
country-specific emission factor was unavailable in the 2025 database. 
Changes in reporting period 
No changes.
Cat 5 Waste generated in own operations 
Relates  to  emissions  from  the  disposal  of  landlord  and  tenant  waste  generated  at 
properties. For non-recycled waste, the waste disposal method is landfill. 
For recycled waste, emissions were computed for recycled paper, metal, plastic, glass, 
e-waste, food waste, and other recycled waste. 
Emission and Conversion factors 
US EPA Emission Factors Hub 2025. 
Changes in reporting period
No changes.
Cat 6 Business travel (air travel)
Relates to emissions from corporate air travel by CLMT employees based on air travel 
distance provided by air travel agency. 
Emission and Conversion factors
UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 2025.
Changes in reporting period
No changes
Cat 13 Downstream leased assets (Landlord and tenant emissions of owned properties 
not accounted for in Scope 1 and 2)
Relates to tenant emissions of CLMT-owned and CLI-operationally managed properties, 
and landlord and tenant emissions of CLMT-owned but third-party operationally managed 
properties.
Emission and Conversion factors 
IEA 2025 v1.1 (AR6 Applied). 
UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 2025.
Changes in reporting period
No changes.

2.	 Ordinary Resolution 1 – Proposed Authority 1
	   	The Proposed Ordinary Resolution 1, if passed, would enable the Manager to allot and issue New Units from time to 
time provided that the aggregate number of the New Units to be issued during the Validity Period, when aggregated 
with the number of units issued during the preceding 12 months must not exceed 20% of the total number of units 
issued in CLMT for the time being.
	   	The Proposed Authority 1 will allow the Manager the flexibility to allot and issue New Units to raise funds to finance 
future investments, acquisitions and capital expenditure to enhance the value of CLMT and/or to refinance existing 
debt as well as for working capital purposes, subject to the relevant laws and regulations. With the Proposed 
Authority 1, delays and further costs involved in convening separate general meetings to approve such issue of New 
Units to raise funds can be avoided. Any allotment and issuance of New Units pursuant to the Proposed Authority 
1 will be subject to the relevant approvals of Securities Commission Malaysia and Bursa Securities.
	   	The Proposed Ordinary Resolution 1 is a renewal of the previous year's mandate. As at the date of this Notice, no 
New Units have been issued pursuant to the mandate granted to the Manager at the previous AGM of CLMT.
3.	 Ordinary Resolution 2 – Proposed Renewal of Unit Buy-Back Mandate
	   	Unitholders are advised to refer to the Statement to Unitholders dated 10 March 2026, which is available on CLMT’s 
website at www.clmt.com.my for further information.
4.	 Ordinary Resolution 3 – Proposed Authority 2
	   	The Proposed Authority 2, if passed, will give authority to the Board to allot and issue the DRP New Units pursuant 
to the DRP upon such terms and conditions and to such persons as the Manager may in its absolute discretion deem 
fit and in the best interest of CLMT and its Unitholders, and such authority shall expire at the conclusion of the next 
AGM of CLMT.
	   	CLMT had applied the DRP to the final income distribution for the period from 1 July 2024 to 31 December 2024 
(2024 Final Income Distribution) which was declared on 22 January 2025. A total of 33,856,268 New Units  were 
issued under the 2024 Final Income Distribution on 17 March 2025 and subsequently, listed on the Main Market of 
Bursa Securities on 19 March 2025. The net proceeds raised from the 2024 Final Income Distribution were utilised 
for working capital and capital expenditure purposes.
	   	CLMT had also applied the DRP to the final income distribution for the period from 7 August 2025 to 31 December 
2025 (2025 Final Income Distribution) which was declared on 28 January 2026. Upon the closing time for submitting 
the distribution reinvestment form on 16 March 2026, the New Units to be issued under the 2025 Final Income 
Distribution will be issued on 25 March 2026 and listed on Main Market of Bursa Securities on 26 March 2026. The 
net proceeds to be raised from the 2025 Final Income Distribution will be utilised for working capital and capital 
expenditure purposes.
	   	The Proposed Authority 2 is a renewal of the previous year's mandate. With Proposed Authority 2, delays and further 
costs involved in convening separate general meetings to approve such issue of New Units can be avoided. If such 
authority is renewed at the forthcoming AGM, any proceeds raised from the issuance(s) of New Units pursuant to 
the Proposed Authority 2 shall be utilised for working capital and capital expenditure purposes.
